img-5.jpeg.description: This is a dependency parsing diagram showing syntactic relationships between words in a sentence. The visualization displays two identical sentences stacked vertically with green lines connecting related words. The sentence reads 'The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just - this is what we are missing, in my opinion. <EOS> <pad>'. The lines represent grammatical dependencies between words, with varying line thickness indicating different types or strengths of relationships. This type of diagram is commonly used in natural language processing (NLP) and computational linguistics to illustrate syntactic structure and word relationships. The special tokens '<EOS>' (end of sentence) and '<pad>' (padding) at the end indicate this is from a machine learning or NLP context where sequences are processed with specific markers.

img-0.jpeg.description: This is an architectural diagram of a Transformer model, showing the encoder-decoder structure. The left side shows the encoder with N× stacked layers, each containing Multi-Head Attention and Feed Forward sublayers with Add & Norm operations. The right side shows the decoder with N× stacked layers, featuring Masked Multi-Head Attention, Multi-Head Attention (for encoder-decoder attention), and Feed Forward sublayers, also with Add & Norm operations. Both sides include Positional Encoding added to Input Embedding (encoder) and Output Embedding (decoder). The decoder processes outputs shifted right. The architecture flows upward through Linear and Softmax layers to produce Output Probabilities. Residual connections are indicated by arrows wrapping around each sublayer block. This diagram represents the standard Transformer architecture used in natural language processing and sequence-to-sequence tasks.

img-1.jpeg.description: This is a computational flow diagram showing the architecture of a neural network attention mechanism, specifically depicting the scaled dot-product attention calculation. The diagram shows a bottom-up flow with three inputs: Q (Query), K (Key), and V (Value). The processing steps are: (1) MatMul operation combining Q and K, (2) Scale operation to normalize the result, (3) optional Mask operation, (4) SoftMax activation function to produce attention weights, and (5) final MatMul operation combining the attention weights with V to produce the output. This is a standard representation of the attention mechanism commonly used in transformer architectures and neural machine translation models.

img-2.jpeg.description: This is an architectural diagram showing the structure of a Scaled Dot-Product Attention mechanism, a fundamental component in transformer neural networks. The diagram shows a bottom-up flow where three inputs (V, K, Q representing Value, Key, and Query) each pass through separate Linear transformation layers. These three linear outputs feed into a central 'Scaled Dot-Product Attention' block (shown in purple/lavender), which has a parameter 'h' indicated on the right side. The attention block outputs multiple parallel streams that converge into a 'Concat' (concatenation) operation, which finally passes through another Linear layer at the top. This represents the multi-head attention architecture where 'h' typically denotes the number of attention heads.

img-3.jpeg.description: This is a comparative diagram showing two parallel text sequences that appear to illustrate changes in legislation or policy language. The top sequence reads 'It is in this spirit that a majority of American governments have passed new laws since 2009 making the registration or voting process more difficult.' The bottom sequence shows similar text with key differences highlighted in colored boxes - notably 'more difficult' is highlighted in red/pink in the bottom version, while appearing in gray in the top. The diagram uses connecting lines to show the relationship between corresponding elements in the two sequences. On the right side, there are multiple instances of '<EOS>' and '<pad>' tokens, suggesting this may be related to natural language processing or text analysis. This visualization appears to demonstrate text comparison, possibly showing original versus modified versions of a statement about voting legislation.

img-4.jpeg.description: This is a linguistic alignment diagram showing word-to-word correspondences between three parallel versions of the same sentence. The diagram uses purple lines of varying opacity to connect corresponding words across the three horizontal text sequences. The sentence reads 'The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just - this is what we are missing, in my opinion. <EOS> <pad>'. The top panel shows a complex many-to-many alignment pattern with multiple crossing lines, the middle panel shows a simplified triangular alignment focusing on key word pairs ('Law' to 'application'), and the bottom panel highlights specific word alignments with colored boxes around 'Law' and 'application'. This type of visualization is commonly used in natural language processing and machine translation research to illustrate how words or phrases correspond across different language versions or text transformations.
